citations.quote: This study has developed tooling for automatically generating system architecture, functions, modes, and components from an initial requirement set. Specifically, a Python tool was developed to couple the Capella MBSE tool to an LLM in order to facilitate a rapid generative design process.

Specifically, the study assesses the ability of LLMs to generate functions, components and modes from system requirements, an activity that in practice typically requires a significant amount of time for a system architect to produce.

The MBSE tool selected for this case study was the Eclipse Foundation's Capella tool (Eclipse 2023). Originally developed by Thales Alenia Space and PolarSys industry working group, this tool offered a powerful Python interface called Python4capella (Labs4Capella 2024). This provided the opportunity for architecture elements generated by an LLM to be fed directly into the system model in Capella. Capella was also selected as it follows the ARCADIA method (Voirin 2023) which is focussed on system architecting.

Therefore, in this study Python was used as the bridge to collect outputs from the LLM and feed them directly into the Capella MBSE tool. This was implemented via a Python package, called NalMage (Neural Network-Assisted Language Modelling for Architecture Generation and Engineering), that included all necessary functions to control interaction with the LLM via OpenAI's API, and generate Capella model elements within the MBSE model, via the Python4Capella API. All interactions with the user, such as entering LLM prompts, were performed via a console within Capella.

The toolchain was configured to mirror classical system architecting processes, and allow user down-selecting at each process stage. The designer inputs requirements, and prompts for the LLM to automatically produce a list of functions that meet them. The user then prompts for a grouping of the generated functions into modes, and then logical components. This process is repeated at each level of the system.

The textual output of the LLM provides the basis of the elements to be added to the MBSE model in Capella. The LLM model was prompted to output lists of suggested elements in bullet point form, allowing simple string splitting, performed by the NALMAGE package, to separate individual model elements down selected by the designer. Then, these elements would be mapped by the NALMAGE package to specific MBSE model types depending on what model element the designer had specified earlier in the prompting process, shown in Figure 3.

The LLM response could include two functions: Image the Earth, and Image the Earth in IR, at which point the designer would select the more detailed second function. This whole process is much quicker than manually identifying each design element and instead allows the designer to simply down select from a list of suggested elements at each stage.

This has been partially reflected in this study by the inclusion of the down selection step after each model element generation stage, that ensures erroneous elements are not carried into the next prompt, but there is the potential for much more in depth user feedback mechanisms to be used.

The tool was applied to three design cases with pre-existing design solutions (which were useful for comparison), with the aim of covering a wide range of different requirement types and wordings. These included: (1) The University of Bristol's CubeSat payload PROVE Pathfinder (Etchells et al. 2022),(Timperley and Berthoud 2022), which was selected as it already had a complete and detailed design with accessible design information, and being a CubeSat mission (i.e.: a nano-spacecraft), complemented the other two full-sized spacecraft missions. (2) A masters' level group design brief for an Earth observation spacecraft that offered an overview of a full sized satellite design with accessible design information. This was an educational example which meant that the requirement wording was considered to be clear and consistent (for the student's benefit), offering perhaps a simpler design case. (3) An industrial study for a European Space Agency Earth Observation (EO) mission, with more limited access to design information. This study was selected as it gives a more 'real-world' industrial example rather than educational examples. Its requirements were much more detailed than the previous two examples.

citations.quote: Traceability was assessed using manual ratings by two human coders, each with several years' experience in systems engineering. The ratings were out of three and performed in accordance with a predefined rule set. This rule set is presented in Table 5 and developed from definitions in (ISO/IEC/IEEE24765:2010(E)2010).
To limit the impact of personal biases in the manual rating, two assessors were used to collect the values for the traceability KPI. Inter-coder reliability was then measured using Cohen's kappa.

The total cost of running these experiments was £10.20 at the time, with 248,270 token prompts used. Assuming roughly similar token costs are maintained, this indicates that prompting cost should not be a barrier to adoption of LLMs in this area, at least for externally hosted models.

It was important to allow the human designer to down select the suggested elements in the LLM output at each stage, as the selected elements of one stage formed the input to the next, therefore poor quality elements would have a snowball effect on the overall design. An example of this is shown in Figure 5 where 3 of 9 top level functions were not decomposed to the next level, as these were not as good quality as the other 6. As a result, human intervention in the process is still important to achieve a good generated design. This study has focused on manually rated assessments. Though this approach was cumbersome to complete, the manual assessments benefited from the experience and detailed knowledge of the assessors. This had the drawback that the rating was sensitive to opinion and biases. As can be seen from Figures 7,8 and Table 6,the assessors had moderate agreement, particularly on alignment scores, however more assessors would have improved the robustness of these assessments.

For example, the inclusion of non-functional requirements will be necessary to ensure that the system not only functions as intended, but also meets the necessary quality standards. It is envisioned that typical methods of non-functional analysis, such as reliability, security or other performance aspects could be leveraged for validation of these requirements and possibly fed back straight to the LLM for correction if non-conformances are identified. For example, mission analysis requirements could be addressed through integration with orbital simulation programmes such as GMAT (NASA - GSFC Open Source Software 2024) or STK (Ansys 2024). The incorporation in the model of interactions and relationships between elements, such as inter-component communication and functional dependencies, would further enhance the completeness of the architectures. When applied to safety-critical systems like spacecraft, this LLM based architecting method may benefit from the inclusion of fault tolerance or identification of alternative system paths (such as degraded modes of operation). While this is currently considered manual work done downstream of the architecture generation presented here and not within the scope of this study, it appears likely that these aspects could be integrated with the LLM prompts for more robust architectures from the beginning. Addressing architecture assessment methods, future work could either include many more assessors to improve the reliability of the rating and/or it should investigate automated alternatives, for example based on cosine similarity with pre-existing designs. This would allow more rapid testing and evaluation of LLMs for design generation. Furthermore, the ontology used to formalise the LLM output into model elements suitable for an MBSE model needs to be refined. More specifically, better control over the semantics of the LLM generated elements is necessary for deep integration with MBSE formalisms seen in languages like SysML. Similarly, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (Fatehkia, Lucas, and Chawla 2024) could be added to control this formalisation of LLM output. The LLM capabilities could be further refined by fine tuning or training on domain-specific knowledge. This may improve its ability to handle long-tail knowledge related to the spacecraft architecting domain, such as payloads and technologies specific to satellites. Direct user feedback mechanisms also offer the potential for improved element generation with an LLM. This work has focused on generating 'baseline' architectures, with simple down selection of LLM-generated elements to combat any errors in output. However, allowing the user to highlight errors or improvements to be made in the LLM output with further prompting would enable iterative improvements directly on the LLM's responses. Performance analysis results or even KPIs, such as the manual traceability presented here or automated KPIs, could be used as part of this feedback process. Automated KPIs typically used to evaluate text generation models do exist, such as; the Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) (Papineni et al. 2002) for assessing the quality of translations, Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (Lin 2004) for summarisation and the Flesch Reading Ease Formula for text readability (Kincaid et al. 1975) (Das and Verma 2020) to name a few. However, each of these are specialised to their particular use case and therefore a new method would need to be developed, applicable to system architecting. Finally, enabling the LLM to react to requirements mid-process could be a highly valuable capability, as mid-project requirement updates are common and lead to costly changes.

The LLM pipeline generated a consistent and acceptable output for 3 different Earth observation spacecraft missions, but human interaction is essential to maintain the quality. Using the LLM made the design process much faster. Some variability can be expected in the output quality for non-deterministic LLMs. More tokens for prompting the LLM will lead to a better output architecture, but the increased cost of doing this should be considered.

For the purposes of this study, text-davinci-003 was selected as the primary LLM, due to its performance and, at the time, it offered larger token limits than other models of similar type. It was also reported to have improved zero-shot capabilities, that was felt to be particularly useful for the purposes of this study. Besides this, it offered close integration with Python and low cost. While much more capable LLMs have since been released, text-davinci-003 was still used to complete all experiments to maintain consistency and it is expected that modern LLM's would likely be just as suitable, if not more.
